new_statements.reading: First-hand phonological analysis (not a grammar): Ancient Greek accent is a pitch/tonal accent (H tone, HL* melody, acute vs circumflex contrasts on long vowels) whose default position is fixed by the recessive rule — penult if the final syllable is heavy, antepenult otherwise, with final consonants extrametrical — and which caps a right-edge three-syllable window for all words; nouns, adjectives and non-finite verbs may carry lexically unpredictable (oxytone/paroxytone) accent within that window. Blumenfeld adds that the lexical phonology is tone-to-stress (a right-edge moraic trochee attracts the HL* fall) while the phrasal component is stress-to-tone with a phrasal default H inserted phrase-finally (his ex. (7)). This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'tonal' coding and its deciding quotation (Kiparsky 2003's recessive-accent statement is the same generalization, with the same final-syllable weight condition). new_statements.rule_in_words: Ancient Greek has a pitch (musical) accent, explicitly contrasted with the stress accent of Modern Greek and English (sec. 151 and N.). The accent is confined to the last three syllables (sec. 149); the antepenult cannot carry it when the ultima is long by nature or position (sec. 163), and final -ai/-oi count as short except in the optative (sec. 169). The KIND of accent (acute/circumflex) follows from syllable quantities (secs. 163-168), but the POSITION 'has to be learned by observation' (sec. 162), i.e. is lexical for nouns and adjectives; verbs, simple or compound, are recessive: the accent goes as far back as the quantity of the last syllable permits, penult quantity disregarded (secs. 159, 178, 423).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the grammar treats proclitics (ten unaccented monosyllables, sec. 179) and enclitics, which throw an additional acute onto a preceding proparoxytone or properispomenon (sec. 183), and the grave as the replacement of a final acute before a following word (sec. 154).
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns in -ews/-ewn (Attic declension, Ionic -ew genitives) allow acute on the antepenult before a long ultima (163 a); recessive accent in composition is 'usually' for nouns/adjectives, 'regularly' for verbs (178); verb exceptions (424-426): enclitic forms of phemi/eimi, five oxytone 2nd-aorist imperatives (eipe, elthe, heure, ide, labe), perispomenon 2nd-aor. middle imperatives, contracted forms, infinitives and participles as verbal nouns with their own fixed accents, the accent not preceding the augment/reduplication in compounds. Dialects (162 D): Aeolic has recessive accent in all words except prepositions and conjunctions; Doric treats final -oi as long and makes certain forms paroxytone/perispomenon.
new_statements.identity_note: Smyth and Goodwin describe classical Attic Greek with Homeric and dialect notes. new_statements.rule_in_words: The Greek accent is a pitch accent ('not simply a stress accent (like ours)'), which sec. 107.1 says only later 'gradually changed to a stress accent' as the language declined. It is restricted to the last three syllables (sec. 106.2); the antepenult cannot be accented if the last syllable is long by nature or ends in xi/psi (sec. 111), final -ai/-oi counting as short except in the optative (sec. 113). For nouns and adjectives the place of the accent in the nominative is lexical ('learned by observation') and the other forms keep that syllable if the ultima permits, otherwise move one syllable forward (sec. 121); verbs generally have recessive accent, including compound verbs (secs. 130, 132).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; proclitics (secs. 136-139) and enclitics (secs. 140-146) are treated, an enclitic giving an extra acute to a preceding proparoxytone/properispomenon.
new_statements.exceptions: Genitives in -eos/-eon of i- and u-stems, the Attic second declension and the Ionic genitive in -eo allow acute on the antepenult before a long ultima (114); oxytone genitives/datives of 1st and 2nd declension are circumflexed (123); monosyllables of the 3rd declension accent the ending in gen./dat. (127) with listed exceptions (128); verb exceptions (131-135): 2nd-aor. active infinitive in -ein and middle imperative in -ou perispomena, five oxytone 2nd-aor. imperatives, contracted mi-optatives, first-aor. and other infinitives on the penult, oxytone participles, the accent not preceding the augment or reduplication in compounds, compounds of dos/es/thes/sches paroxytone; participles inflect like adjectives (134).

tone_statements.citation: Golston, Chris & Christian Paulsen. 2026. Ancient Greek Nominal Accentuation. Proceedings of the Annual UCLA Indo-European Conference 35(1). eScholarship, University of California.
tone_statements.quote: The prosody of Ancient Greek involves a delicate interplay between stress (Allen 1973) and pitch accent (Sauzet 1989). ... The pitch accent is generally positioned relative to the word stress. The position of pitch accent is of course marked orthographically in Greek with either an acute or circumflex over the vowel. A circumflex indicates a falling contour HL and we assume that an acute represents a level high tone both on short vowels and on long ... The HL pitch accent is a falling contour either across (γάλα [ˈɡálà] ‘milk’) or within syllables (συκῆ [suuˈkέὲ] ‘fig tree’).
tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent (acute = H, circumflex = HL over two morae; one H per word; separate final low boundary tone) placed relative to an independent weight-based stress on the last two syllables.

tone_statements.citation: Gunkel, Dieter. 2023. Musical Evidence for Low Boundary Tones in Ancient Greek. Greek and Roman Musical Studies 11(2): 231-284.
tone_statements.quote: the accent of a penultimate syllable in ancient Greek is realized as a circumflex (HL) if and only if the penultimate syllable contains a long vowel or diphthong and the vowel of the final syllable is short (1ab); otherwise, the accent is realized as an acute (H) (1cd). ... This invites an explanation in terms of tone, because the tone bearing units of the language are vowels and diphthongs. ... I will adopt a tonal analysis of ancient Greek accent based primarily on Golston 1990. – circumflex = HL – persistent (lexically inherent) acute = H – recessive (phonologically derived) acute = HL*
tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent: acute (H) vs circumflex (HL), contrasting only on word-final VV-syllables; argues from Delphic hymns for a word/clitic-group-final low boundary tone; grave = lowered or deleted H.

sources.quote: By contrast, the position of the ancient Greek accent is not predictable from the shape of a word alone, and yet there are some restrictions on its placement -- some positions in the word where (with one limited group of exceptions) we can be sure not to find the accent. These restrictions are known collectively as the 'law of limitation', and may be stated as follows: The accent does not fall further from the end of the word than the antepenultimate syllable, or the penultimate if the final syllable is heavy. For the purposes of this law, a single word-final consonant does not count towards syllable weight.

sources.quote: The prosody of Ancient Greek involves a delicate interplay between stress (Allen 1973) and pitch accent (Sauzet 1989). ... The pitch accent is generally positioned relative to the word stress. The position of pitch accent is of course marked orthographically in Greek with either an acute or circumflex over the vowel. A circumflex indicates a falling contour HL and we assume that an acute represents a level high tone both on short vowels and on long ... The HL pitch accent is a falling contour either across (γάλα [ˈɡálà] ‘milk’) or within syllables (συκῆ [suuˈkέὲ] ‘fig tree’).
